extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners studying humor genres (comedians, comedy writers, cultural historians)
extracted.subtask_description: Describe or identify ribaldry (aka blue comedy/bawdiness) by its defining features, typical contexts, and distinctions from related comedic subgenres. Useful for writers, performers, critics, and students analyzing off-color humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ribaldry / blue comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribaldry, also known as blue comedy, is a humorous genre of entertainment that ranges from bordering on indelicacy to indecency, with the humorous elements based on amusingly coarse and morally incorrect or irreverent talk and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often called 'bawdiness' or 'bawdy'; may be read as conventional or subversive. Examples include classical works (Aristophanes, Plautus), medieval and modern literature, and certain films and comic works. Use this definition to classify material that foregrounds coarse/irreverent sexual talk or behavior as ribaldry rather than as purely erotic/pornographic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on shared sexual conventions and taboo-breaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribaldry typically depends on a shared background of sexual conventions and values, and its comedy generally depends on seeing those conventions broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ritual taboo-breaking underlies ribaldry's controversial nature and explains why it can provoke censorship. When evaluating ribald material, consider whether humor arises from recognition of social/sexual norms and their deliberate transgression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aim is comic commentary, not sexual stimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex is presented in ribald material more for the purpose of poking fun at the foibles and weaknesses that manifest themselves in human sexuality, rather than to present sexual stimulation either overtly or artistically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether sexual content is being used to satirize or comment on human behavior (qualifies as ribaldry) versus being primarily intended for arousal (leans toward erotica/pornography). Ribaldry may also use sex as a metaphor to illustrate non-sexual concerns, bordering on satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and content markers (off-colour, risqué, indecent, profane)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blue comedy is comedy that is off-colour, risqué, indecent, or profane, largely about sex. It often contains profanity or sexual imagery that may shock and offend some audience members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these tone markers when classifying a performer or piece as 'blue' — presence of profanity, explicit sexual imagery, or intentionally shocking sexual references are indicators. Examples: comedians described as 'blue' or routines labeled 'working blue.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Working blue (performance practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Working blue' refers to the act of using swear words and discussing things that people would not discuss in 'polite society'. A 'blue comedian' usually performs risqué routines layered with curse words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider context: many comedians alternate between family-friendly public personas and blue material in adult-oriented/private settings. Historical anecdotes (Masquers roasts, midnight shows) illustrate this private/public dichotomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual/social settings for bawdy song and blue material
rubrics_metrics.description: Bawdy songs are humorous songs that emphasize sexual themes and are often rich with innuendo; historically these songs tend to be confined to groups of young males, either as students or in an environment where alcohol is flowing freely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a bawdy song/function is tied to group rituals (student songs, sailors' songs, rugby songs, Hash House Harriers). Context (private drinking groups vs public performance) affects whether material is experienced as ribald tradition or censurable obscenity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from black comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribaldry differs from black comedy in that the latter deals with topics that would normally be considered painful or frightening, whereas ribaldry deals with topics that would only be considered offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying humor, determine whether the subject matter invokes morbidity/pain (black comedy) or primarily sexual/offensive transgression (ribaldry). This distinction affects critical framing and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and broadcast constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of blue comedy over American radio airwaves is severely restricted due to decency regulations; the Federal Communications Commission can levy fines against radio stations that air obscene content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for legal/regulatory limits and platform rules when assessing suitability for broadcast or public distribution. Material acceptable in private club roasts or adult venues may be prohibited or fined on regulated airwaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/literary scope and demographics of blue literature
rubrics_metrics.description: As a part of English literature, blue literature dates back to at least Middle English, with bawdy humor central to writers such as Shakespeare and Chaucer. Until the 1940s, writers of English-language blue literature were almost exclusively men; since then women have been able to build commercial careers on blue literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical examples (Rabelais, Chaucer, Swift, Twain) and demographic notes when situating a work within a tradition. Consider authorship, cultural context, and changes over time when evaluating how a text fits the blue-literature category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career/genre specialization (performers who build careers on blue comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some comedians build their careers on blue comedy; notable examples include Redd Foxx, Lawanda Page, and Dave Attell. Specific cultural forms (e.g., African American signifying/toasting) constitute distinct blue performance traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing performers, consider whether their material is consistently blue and whether they operate within a recognized subtradition (e.g., signifying). Career trajectory and audience base can indicate whether a performer is primarily a 'blue comic.'
